headline: Cloud coding agent acts like an autonomous engineer, not a pair programmer, completing complex tasks independently
summary: A first run with Cursor Cloud Agent revealed it operates in a fresh, isolated environment, autonomously setting up monorepos and creating pull requests, unlike a continuous local session.
details: The first interaction with a cloud coding agent, specifically Cursor Cloud Agent, demonstrated a surprising level of autonomy, feeling more like hiring an engineer than pair programming. It successfully executed a complex task on a real monorepo with minimal user intervention.

The agent started in a fresh environment, performed onboarding, installed dependencies, ran tests, and even played a solo turn in a UI. It then opened a pull request with documentation and a verification trail, showcasing its ability to establish a complete execution environment.

Crucially, the cloud agent did not inherit the local session's context, planning, or authenticated tools. Decisions and reasoning made locally had to be re-established, highlighting a distinct execution model separate from continuous local workflows.

This clean-environment approach means cloud agents excel at bounded jobs with clear definitions of done, rather than open-ended design debates. Effective use requires an explicit handoff of context, similar to briefing a new team member.

While a local git worktree offers parallel execution and reuses existing tools, it couples results to the developer's machine. The cloud agent, despite requiring more explicit context, provides an isolated, reproducible task that reduces "works on my machine" risks.

The experience with Cursor clearly illustrates an architectural boundary: autonomous coding agents require explicit handoff and clean environments. This trade-off between inherited state and isolated execution is expected to be a common theme as coding agents become more independent.

headline: Amazon AWS revenue up 37%, investors favor cloud hosts in AI boom
summary: Amazon reported strong Q2 earnings, with AWS revenue up 37% year-over-year. The company is significantly increasing its data center spending, raising its 2026 capex forecast to $220 billion, signaling investor confidence in AI infrastructure.
details: Amazon's second-quarter earnings exceeded expectations, with net sales rising 20% and cloud revenue emerging as a particular strong point. This positive performance was enough to send Amazon's stock up nearly 10% in after-hours trading.

The company is not slowing down on data center spending, despite conventional wisdom suggesting investors want companies to rein it in. Amazon spent $173 billion on property and equipment for the fiscal year ended June 30, a significant increase from $107.65 billion the previous year.

Amazon also raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast from $200 billion to $220 billion, even as it began using its cash reserves to cover costs. AWS revenue grew 37% year-over-year, clocking $42 billion for the quarter, which helps justify the massive infrastructure investment.

Beyond data centers, Amazon is making long-term bets on chips like the Trainium TPU and the Arm-based Graviton processor. These projects aim to meaningfully improve margins for the company's cloud business, with CEO Andy Jassy anticipating a similar margin trajectory to the core business.

This trend extends beyond Amazon, with Microsoft and Google also seeing stock increases after reporting strong cloud revenue. In contrast, companies like Meta, with significant capital expenditure and less clear AI revenue sources, are facing intense investor skepticism.

Investors are currently treating cloud hosts as the most reliable part of the AI stack, while remaining skeptical about the underlying economics for AI labs and startups. The sustainability of spending by major AI labs and their clients will ultimately determine the stability of revenue for cloud hosts like Amazon.
